title: Hybrid admission + preemptive dequeue to stop small-request drowning during multi-tenant bursts
creator: Aisha Khan
description: Summary: Several Dedicated customers and one Hosted account reported repeated high tail latency for short/interactive requests when the cluster experienced bursts of long-context generations from other tenants. Symptoms surfaced as: sudden per-tenant queue depth spikes, elevated p50->p99 latency divergence for short requests, frequent KV cache evictions, and visible backlog amplification in the batching scheduler. Root cause: the admission controller used a throughput-weighted token accounting that prioritized high-token long requests during throttle windows. When a burst occurred, long requests occupied batching slots and prevented the scheduler from forming low-latency small-request batches; these small requests aged and became starved. Secondary effect: aggressive KV eviction for active large contexts caused cache churn that further amplified service time for subsequent requests. Goal: implement a hybrid admission policy that factors request length, request age, and latency sensitivity tag; add preemptive dequeue and short-request fast-path to ensure bounded tail for interactive flows; adjust KV eviction heuristics to preserve prefixes pinned by active small flows.
comments: 2026-02-11 - Aisha K: Initial customer escalation received from CS (ticket CS-3489, Dedicated customer 'BrightForms') reporting intermittent p99 spikes for short chat completions while nightly batch jobs ran. Reproduced on staging with synthetic mix (90% small, 10% long) and observed starvation pattern.

2026-02-13 - Miguel O: Root-cause hypothesis established after correlating ingress timestamps, admission token consumption, and batch composition. Long requests consume token buckets faster and prevent small-request batches when cluster is near capacity. Logged reproducer and perf trace (trace id trace-20260213-7b9).

2026-02-18 - Engineering: Implemented prototype hybrid admission controller (length + age weighting) and a preemptive-dequeue path for latency-tagged requests. Benchmarked in local CI: p99 for small requests improved from 420ms to 85ms under synthetic burst, throughput loss <2% for long workloads.

2026-02-21 - QA: Added deterministic replay test using recorded production traces (customer anonymized). Found an edge case where very old small-requests correctly prioritized but then hit a race with KV handoff; added a short mutex around handoff to prevent double-eviction.
2026-02-25 - Infra: Created canary pool 'dedicated-burst-canary' and runtime flag rollout plan. Canary will start at 2 nodes in us-west-2, then scale to 10 nodes if metrics stable for 12 hours.

2026-03-01 - PR: Opened change PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/12877. Contents: hybrid admission implementation, preemptive dequeue scheduler hook, KV eviction tweak, and telemetry additions. Requesting review from @clairechen and @rajiv-s.

2026-03-03 - Metrics: Added Grafana panels and alert 'ShortRequestTailHigh' (prom alert expr: increase(queue_short_requests[5m]) > 50 AND histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(request_duration_bucket{type="short"}[5m])) > 0.3). Alert documented in runbook RB-612.

2026-03-05 - Customer mitigation: Applied temporary ingress shaping for affected tenants (CS action) to limit concurrent long-context submissions; mitigated customer-visible p99 spikes while fix is validated.

2026-03-09 - Code review: Addressed feedback about fairness proofs and added unit tests covering mixed-size scheduling and starvation scenarios. Added a feature flag runtime.hybrid_admission_v2 to gate rollout.

2026-03-11 - Canary rollout: Deployed to 'dedicated-burst-canary' (2 nodes). Observed p99 drop for short requests from 420ms -> 78ms. No increase in 95th/mean latency for long requests. No KV eviction rate anomalies. Proceeding to broaden canary.
2026-03-12 - Rollout decision: Expand to 20% of Dedicated capacity and enable on Hosted read-only for telemetry. Notify SEs and CSMs of planned lift to full rollout pending 48h stability window.
